items.finding: Preregistered analysis of 22,031 Day Reconstruction Method episodes from 2,508 Germans aged 17–95, drawn from the German Socio-Economic Panel across four waves. Multilevel logistic models showed being alone consistently raised the odds of feeling lonely, and people were lonelier at home than at work or elsewhere. Watching television raised it; self-care and media use lowered it. Duration mattered too: prolonged care work increased loneliness, while prolonged social contact decreased it.
items.why: Your slides frame loneliness dispositionally (“often have average # of friends”). This makes it a context-driven state with teachable triggers — and lonelier at home than at work is a genuinely counterintuitive opener.

items.finding: Two online studies separating relationship happiness from relationship meaningfulness. In Study 1 (n = 426), greater sexual desire and satisfaction and fewer sacrifices and less stress predicted happiness but were unrelated to meaningfulness; greater negative self-disclosure to a partner predicted meaningfulness but not happiness. Study 2 (n = 711) replicated this and found that people who prefer a meaningful relationship over a happy one report higher satisfaction, optimism, closeness and forgiveness, and less stress.
items.why: Your Social Exchange slides treat satisfaction as one quantity (Outcomes vs. CL). This splits the outcome in two and shows the costs that reduce happiness can build meaning — a direct complication of the rewards/costs ledger.

items.finding: Five studies testing whether people can actually detect when someone else feels authentic. In acquainted dyads, romantic partners read each other accurately after making sacrifices (Study 1) and after discussing personal distress and desired change (Study 2), but failed when discussing relationship conflict (Study 3) — the authors attribute this to the high interpersonal stakes. In Studies 4A and 4B, outside observers watching thin-slice videos of those same conflict conversations did detect the differences the partners had missed.
items.why: A clean boundary condition for your “Accuracy of Partner Perceptions” slides, and the thin-slice result links back to the 0.1-second first impression material earlier in the same lecture.

items.finding: Connects truth-default theory, developed in deception research, to the misinformation literature. TDT predicts findings misinformation scholars found surprising — notably that relatively few people are exposed to or share misinformation online. It also cuts the other way: TDT's claim that people are reflexively truth-biased is challenged by misinformation results. The authors argue deception-detection paradigms clarify how detection studies should be designed (true–false base rates, prompted versus unprompted judgments) and how to improve detection without eroding trust in credible news.
items.why: You already teach truth bias and the finance-lie study where 0% detected deception. This names the theory organizing those findings and bridges to material students care about.

items.finding: Introductory psychology students at a Canadian university each recruited a significant other — a romantic partner, a close friend, or a primary caregiver — giving 308 dyads who completed self-esteem and relationship-quality measures. Actor–Partner Interdependence analyses replicated Robinson and Cameron's 2012 romantic finding and extended it: the higher the two members' combined self-esteem, the higher the quality of the relationship at the dyad level. Self-esteem appears to work as a shared resource across all three relationship types, not just romantic ones.
items.why: Your partner-feedback material (self-verification vs. self-enhancement) is romantic-only. This licenses extending it to friendship, where Lecture 7 already lives.

items.finding: Experimental work linking musical synchrony to social bonding has run almost entirely on Western participants, and critics have questioned both its cross-cultural generality and whether music is doing the causal work. The "Many Voices" Registered Reports, co-designed with over 100 collaborators, tested it at scale: group singing enhanced social bonding significantly more than speaking did, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. The authors draw out lessons for evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, and argue that collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers does not dilute the science but improves it.
items.why: A strong companion to your ape-grooming and physical-support sequence — and it answers the cross-cultural objection directly.

items.finding: Draws on Self-Determination Theory and the Discrepancy Model of Loneliness to treat loneliness as what happens when a relationship fails to meet the need for relatedness. In a survey of 546 people, both perceived partner materialism and one's own materialism were associated with greater loneliness — pointing to unmet expectations for closeness rather than mismatched values as the driver. Perceived partner materialism related to higher relationship satisfaction only among people who were themselves materialistic. Both perceived partner materialism and loneliness were associated with compulsive buying and a tendency to hold onto products, even controlling for personal materialism.
items.why: Loneliness inside a relationship is a good way into comparison level and unmet expectations.

items.finding: Most evidence that narcissism breeds aggression comes from cross-sectional, between-person studies of Western convenience samples. This preregistered study used four large Chinese data sets instead: ambulatory assessment of 427 undergraduates and 775 offenders (19,331 and 42,820 observations) plus two longitudinal samples assessed four times over a year. Narcissism and aggression prospectively predicted each other at the momentary level but not the long-term level, and the reciprocal pattern largely replicated across students and offenders. Higher person-level aggression consistently strengthened the effect of narcissistic states on later aggression among offenders. The authors present this as the first within-person evidence for the dynamic.
items.why: Refines the blunt “narcissists are aggressive” claim into a within-person, momentary process — and directly answers the WEIRD-sample objection.

items.finding: The gratitude list is among the best-studied well-being interventions, but what people actually write down had gone largely unexamined. Natural language processing applied to a global online study of 19,265 people identified 16 thematic clusters, the most common centered on social relationships. Content varied by sociodemographic and psychological characteristics. Crucially for practice, mentioning family or nature was associated with larger increases in positivity after the activity — suggesting the intervention could be personalized rather than delivered generically.
items.why: A concrete maintenance behavior with large-sample backing for your cognitive-strategies section.

items.finding: Sexual objectification is well established as harmful to the people objectified. This theoretical article asks a question psychology has rarely posed: what does it cost the objectifier? Drawing on social, cognitive, organizational and relationship science, the authors argue objectifying others compromises one's own capacity to form close relationships, collaborate effectively and function socially and professionally. Four mechanisms are proposed — cognitive load, a face–body attentional trade-off, goal-based perception, and dehumanization — operating as parallel, mutually reinforcing pathways that converge on social miscalibration. They frame this as an additional reason to reduce objectification, complementing rather than replacing concern for its targets.
items.why: A useful counterweight to lectures built largely around physical mate-preference findings.

items.finding: Tests whether the Marital Offense-Specific Forgiveness Scale measures the same thing across religious groups, using 935 adults recruited from Catholic and Muslim congregations in Germany (287 Muslim, 648 Christian). Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis supported the two-factor structure — Benevolence and Resentment/Avoidance — and established configural, metric and partial scalar invariance, enough for meaningful cross-group comparison, though full scalar and residual invariance were not achieved. Latent mean analysis found significantly higher resentment/avoidance among Christian participants, with no group difference in Benevolence.
items.why: Measurement support for the forgiveness construct you teach in two separate lectures.

items.finding: Asks why researchers reading the same evidence disagree about whether social media harms adolescent mental health, and points to two analytic habits. First, studies usually report correlation coefficients alone rather than elevated risk, which is easier to misread. Second, they blend heterogeneous exposures (lumping digital activities together, television watching included), outcomes (depression with life satisfaction) and populations (girls with boys), then treat the weak aggregate association as evidence that specific risks are negligible. The authors show how sequential blending can turn a large, clinically relevant association into a negligible one, and urge reporting in terms of elevated risk and examining heterogeneity across platforms, usage levels and populations.
items.why: Present as a live methodological dispute, not settled fact. This is one side of an active argument about how to analyze the same body of evidence.
items.caution: One side of an active methodological dispute. Present as contested, not settled.

items.finding: Three major accounts of why humans bond to groups have developed largely in parallel: the social cohesion approach, the social identity approach, and identity fusion theory. Each has empirical support, and nobody had tried to reconcile them. This review proposes a general framework specifying what each approach uniquely contributes, which psychological phenomena each best explains, and where their apparent inconsistencies can be resolved. The authors then advance a network model setting out how different aspects of the self-concept give rise to group connection.
items.why: Background reading if you want to tighten the belonging material.

items.finding: Asks whether insecure attachment predicts social anxiety specifically in situations involving one's own romantic partner, and whether dyadic coping explains the link. A community sample of 88 adults in relationships completed attachment measures, rated their partner's dyadic coping style, and took a newly developed measure of partner-specific social anxiety. Both attachment anxiety and avoidance were positively associated with social anxiety around the partner. Perceived *negative* dyadic coping partially mediated those associations, while perceived supportive coping did not — suggesting it is the partner's unhelpful responses to stress, rather than the absence of helpful ones, that carries the effect.
items.why: N=88 community convenience sample. On-topic for your attachment slides but cite cautiously.

items.finding: Meta-analysis of 457 independent samples from 302 studies, total N = 244,257. Situational judgment tests predicted not only job performance but also academic performance, organizational citizenship behavior and counterproductive work behavior, and validity was higher in real applicant settings than in research settings. Newer formats held up: multimedia SJTs matched text-based validity at lower cognitive load, multiple-choice did not outperform written constructed responses, and webcam-recorded responses carried the lowest cognitive load of all. The authors discuss cost-effectiveness against other selection methods.
items.why: Your selection lecture covers biodata, work samples, references, background checks, cybervetting and interviews — but not SJTs, now among the best-evidenced tools available. Your closing slide asks how interviews can be improved; this is the missing third answer, with the largest N in the batch.

items.finding: BERTopic modeling of 5,865 empirical articles published in the Journal of Applied Psychology from its 1917 founding through June 2024, yielding 99 topics across 25 higher-order themes. Five themes bear directly on social impact: workplace stress and well-being; diversity, equity and inclusion; organizational justice and legal issues; employment transitions across the lifespan; and social justice and labor opinions. Trends from 1980 to 2024 show health and well-being research growing, DEI scholarship holding steady, justice and legal topics rising then falling, and labor-related research disappearing altogether.
items.why: A far better “History of I/O” slide than Yerkes and WW1 testing alone — a data-driven century of the field’s own priorities. The vanishing of labor research also speaks to your Lecture 5 claim about pensions and union power.

items.finding: Ten-day daily diary study of 149 UK full-time employees who used generative AI at work daily or more (mean age 36.7, 63.8% male), building on self-determination theory and the job crafting literature. Four crafting dimensions — augmenting instrumental resources, augmenting social resources, augmenting challenging demands, and automating hindering demands — were linked to daily engagement through need satisfaction and then work meaningfulness. The competence pathway drew the most consistent support and relatedness the least. In open-ended responses, employees described automating drudgery as a deliberate reallocation of attention toward work they valued rather than simply doing less.
items.why: Your AI lecture rests on E0/E1/E2 exposure and EPOCH, both conceptual. This is empirical evidence about what employees actually do with AI, and it maps onto the Job Characteristics Model you already teach.

items.finding: Tests a cornerstone claim that self-determination theory has asserted for three decades but never properly examined: that autonomy, competence and relatedness are *necessary* for well-being, not merely correlated with it. The authors argue regression-based methods cannot answer this because they express an average-effect logic, and instead apply Necessary Condition Analysis. Across three studies all three needs were confirmed as necessary for evaluative well-being (job satisfaction and work meaningfulness), affective well-being (positive affect) and conative well-being (work engagement), with some variation in how strongly. Power and status were not necessary.
items.why: This strengthens your SDT slide rather than undermining it, and gives a sharp methods aside: “necessary” and “correlated on average” are different claims needing different statistics.

items.finding: Cross-lagged meta-analytic structural equation models synthesizing over 3,000 correlations from longitudinal studies, representing more than 11,000 teams. Emergent states and processes showed inertia, but unevenly: conflict was the stickiest construct and affect the least. Team affect and cognition tended to coevolve with team processes, while motivation and conflict were consistently predicted by earlier processes. Team performance formed feedback loops, predicting later states and processes which in turn predicted later performance. The interval between observations moderated all of this.
items.why: Your teamwork material is static — problems and fixes. “Conflict is the stickiest thing in a team” is memorable and actionable next to your social-loafing remedies.

items.finding: A curated set of 40 questions on diversity, equity and inclusion in organizations, crowdsourced from the authors' professional networks and answered from current literature, aimed squarely at the myths and misperceptions that circulate about DEI's role in I/O psychology and management. The questions are organized into themes: foundations of DEI, the business case, DEI effectiveness, DEI resistance, legal interpretations, DEI pullback, measurement, and programs and vehicles. The authors are explicit that it is not comprehensive, but it is built to answer the questions people actually raise.
items.why: Maps almost slide-for-slide onto your equality/equity/justice and affirmative-action sequence.

items.finding: Starts from the observation that most attempts at inclusive culture change have either not worked or actively backfired, and argues the common fault is treating culture as the sum of individual effort while underestimating situations. The review disaggregates situational power into four distinct types of force, drawing on social psychology and adjacent fields, and shows that some push beliefs, behaviors, interactions and relationships toward inclusion while others push the opposite way. A central aim is to trace how individual beliefs and behaviors connect upward into changes in local culture, and to mark where the research is still missing.
items.why: Your slide asks “Problems with equity?” and lists outcomes. This supplies the mechanisms behind why efforts stall or backfire.

items.finding: Most recovery research studies evening activities one at a time. This work instead differentiates seven characteristics — physical, social, creative, mental, spiritual, virtual and outdoor — and takes a person-centered approach to find how they co-occur. Two 10-day daily diary studies were used: Study 1 (N = 345, 1,907 observations) identified daily recovery profiles and linked them to recovery experiences, emotional exhaustion and next-morning vigor; Study 2 (N = 321, 1,780 observations) tested whether those profiles replicated in an independent sample and added work-related antecedents and next-day outcomes. The profiles largely held up across samples and each related distinctly to well-being and work outcomes.
items.why: An evidence-based upgrade to your “Environmental Destressors: nature, music, pets” slide.

items.finding: Theorizes that prosocial motivation gives women a role-congruent route to becoming valued advice sources, drawing on social role theory and role congruity theory. In a time-lagged, multi-source field study (n = 275), women occupied less central positions in workplace advice networks than men, but high prosocial motivation closed that gap. Advice centrality then mediated the combined effect of gender and prosocial motivation on leadership emergence and performance ratings. Two online experiments (n = 247; n = 248) provided converging causal evidence. The authors note the uncomfortable implication: parity here may rest on demands that fall asymmetrically on women.
items.why: Good companion to your Intel “Well Done!” recognition study — and the title’s “carrying the burden” is the point worth discussing.

items.finding: Challenges the "model minority" framing by disaggregating a category usually treated as a monolith. Study 1 examined CEOs and CFOs of FTSE companies across 14 years (2011–2024): there were virtually no ethnic Chinese in those roles, while ethnic Indian representation did not differ significantly from Whites. Study 2 used the UK Biobank (N = 322,734) and found the effect was moderated by gender — ethnic Chinese men were significantly less likely than ethnic Indian and White men to reach leadership, partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance, while ethnic Chinese, Indian and White women did not differ from one another and were each disadvantaged relative to men. Results held across survey-based and polygenic measures of risk tolerance.
items.why: A vivid lesson in why disaggregating a demographic category matters — fits your adverse-impact and diversity material.

items.finding: Reviews a decade of work built on the conflict expression framework, which holds that what matters is not only what a conflict is about but how it is voiced. Expressions vary along two dimensions: directness and oppositional intensity. Three propositions follow — that the effects of a conflict depend on how it is expressed, that members of the same group perceive the same conflict differently, and that conflict moves negotiation dynamically through statements and the responses they draw. The review covers empirical tests of these propositions, methodological advances, and the framework's wider use as a foundation for conflict communication research.
items.why: A more current taxonomy than the five resolution styles alone.

items.finding: Surveys a decade of misinformation research, separating settled ground from live dispute across definitions, measurement and theory. The authors argue susceptibility is best assessed as the ability to tell true claims from false ones rather than belief in falsehoods, and note that outright fake-news exposure online is rarer than commonly assumed even though misinformation more broadly construed remains a serious problem. They review the cognitive and socio-affective mechanisms behind susceptibility — repetition effects, weak analytic reasoning, political identity, information environments — and evaluate the main interventions: fact-checking, prebunking, psychological inoculation and accuracy prompts.
items.why: Speaks directly to your confirmation-bias and attitude-polarization slides.

items.finding: Argues that the satisfaction-optimized design of LLMs produces "suppressed inquiry": the tools inhibit rather than support a user's questioning. They appear fluent and all-knowing, which makes non-LLM work feel tedious by comparison; they affirm rather than interrogate assumptions, yielding output that is deceptively adequate — shallower and less carefully reasoned than it looks; their apparent competence reduces the vigilance independent judgment requires; and their framing narrows what users think to ask. These costs are self-concealing, since noticing them demands the very engagement being suppressed, and repeated delegation gradually erodes the capacity to reason alone. Three pressures make correction hard: commercial incentives rewarding satisfaction over substance, models reverting to agreeable defaults even when pushed, and a broader drift toward less effortful engagement.
items.why: Excellent in-class discussion piece for a room full of AI users.

items.finding: Inclusive leadership is usually theorized through its benefits, leaving out what leaders actually run into. This inductive study of 47 historically marginalized STEM employees and 14 leaders they named as inclusive models it as a three-part process: inclusion efforts (attentive learning, talent amplification, structural debiasing); the resistance those efforts draw (skepticism, gatekeeping, fit critiques, non-compliance); and strategies to mitigate that resistance (explaining value, co-crafting strategies, evaluating fit critiques, managing change momentum). The authors tested boundary conditions against three further STEM samples — racial minority men, lower-ranking women, and White males. The first two replicated the model; the third suggested White men perceive inclusive leadership differently.
items.why: Adds the resistance half of the story to your leadership styles material.

items.finding: Offers a cognitive-ecological explanation for why stereotype content skews negative. Cognitively, people characterize a group by the attributes that distinguish it from other groups. Ecologically, positive social information is more frequent while negative information is more diverse — so negative attributes, being rarer and more varied, are more likely to distinguish one group from another. The authors demonstrate the predicted negativity across two studies and two existing data sets, then formalize the theory with simulations showing that rare attributes can be highly diagnostic of group membership while applying to only a minority of members. Notably, the account needs no motivational derogation, no essentialism and no general negativity bias.
items.why: A mechanism for the hiring-bias findings you already present as empirical facts.

items.finding: Fifteen empathy researchers set out to fix a problem that has dogged the field since the word was coined: "empathy" is used as an umbrella for a range of distinct processes, which muddles communication among scholars, practitioners and the public. They produced a shared lexicon of lower-order constructs — vicarious affect, emotional contagion, emotion co-sharing, sympathy/compassion, personal distress, perspective taking, accurate inference, mimicry, synchrony, projection and transportation. Their recommendation is that this more specific vocabulary be used routinely and the umbrella term sparingly.
items.why: Useful for sharpening what the E in EPOCH actually denotes.

items.finding: Integrates cross-domain spillover and regulatory focus theory to ask whether watching your own investments move affects how you behave at work. In a 10-day experience sampling study of full-time employees who personally invest in the South Korean stock market, a more positive than usual morning fluctuation in holdings predicted higher state risk propensity, which in turn produced more risk-taking behavior and more voice. The effect was moderated by long-term orientation, with employees lower in it more sensitive to the morning swing. Two follow-up experiments supported the proposed mechanism, showing positive fluctuations elicited promotion focus and negative ones prevention focus.
items.why: A memorable cross-domain spillover example for motivation or attitudes.

items.finding: Takes stock of decades of evidence that women initiate fewer negotiations and perform less competitively, along with moderators such as structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience, and anticipated backlash as the proposed mechanism. Recent findings are mixed: gaps in negotiation behavior still replicate, but gaps in propensity to initiate and moderation by representation role often do not, and some studies find an outright reversal, with women more likely than men to negotiate in certain situations and female counterparts liked more, producing greater counterpart satisfaction. The authors flag statistical power as a likely source of inconsistency given the small-to-medium effects typical here, and conclude that performance gaps persist while propensity gaps have largely closed.
items.why: Good for teaching that evidence moves — not every classic finding holds.

items.finding: Revisits the Queen Bee phenomenon — senior women in male-dominated settings distancing from junior women, aligning with masculine norms and downplaying gender inequality. Rather than a character flaw, the review casts it as a way of coping with gendered organizational contexts and constrained advancement that provoke social identity threat. It is modeled as a socially embedded, self-reinforcing feedback loop: coping responses that may pay off for the individual in the short run while undermining solidarity, legitimizing inequality and reducing pressure for structural change. The authors situate it alongside related strategies including code-switching, identity bifurcation and assimilation, and argue for fixing systems rather than individuals.
items.why: Shifts the phenomenon from individual failing to structural response.

items.finding: Argues executive retirement differs from ordinary retirement and should be read in an achievement context, drawing on late adulthood developmental psychology. Firm performance is proposed to work through two mechanisms — legacy fulfillment, salient when performance is high, and selective prioritization, salient when it is low — which together produce a U-shaped relationship between firm performance and the likelihood of retiring. Achievement goal orientations serve as boundary conditions probing those mechanisms. The authors found general support using an archival dataset of 1,840 CEOs from S&P 1500 firms and a two-wave survey of 363 executives.
items.why: Late-career material for your careers lecture, which currently stops at entry.

items.finding: No abstract is published in any open source, since Elsevier deposits none — only the title, authors and journal are available. From the title, the study concerns how people react psychologically to subordinates using large language models at work, which sits directly on the AI material in the Future of I-O lecture and the leadership unit. Worth retrieving the full text through the library if the topic fits.
items.why: No abstract available in any open source (Elsevier deposits none). Highly on-topic for your AI lecture — worth retrieving through the library.
items.caution: No abstract in any open source (Elsevier deposits none). Title and authors only — retrieve through the library.

items.finding: Researchers collected 393 anonymized emails written in French and English by 14–16-year-olds to a recognized youth support organization, then put each question to ChatGPT-3.5 over two weeks in January 2024 using a netnography approach. 17.8% of the emails were flagged as potentially violating the content policy. Answers that did come through followed a consistent shape: an introduction restating the question, normalizing the experience and validating emotions; a list of recommendations; and a close encouraging help-seeking. The recommendations pushed authenticity, personal agency, self-care, open communication and seeking support.
items.why: Your lectures argue “porn is becoming the new sex education.” The sequel is already here. The 17.8% refusal rate is the number that lands: the tool is least available exactly where teens most need it.

items.finding: 266 students at a southeastern U.S. university read three sexual-health passages — on sexual communication, body image, and sexual pleasure and safety — that were word-for-word identical across conditions. Only the stated author varied: generative AI, an academic expert, a community health professional, or a peer/social media influencer. The AI-attributed version scored lower on every outcome measured: perceived accuracy and clarity, warmth and helpfulness, trustworthiness, self-efficacy and willingness to act. Source effects on willingness to act were largest for pleasure and safety and smallest for communication, and held after controlling for students' own AI familiarity and attitudes.
items.why: A clean source-credibility experiment on your own student population, rhyming with the source-credibility material in PSY170 Lecture 11. Teachable conclusion: AI works best paired with a human.

items.finding: A 2025 nationally representative online survey of 1,259 English-speaking 15–29-year-olds assigned female at birth, fielding a newly developed measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies for the first time. Among the 633 who had had penile-vaginal sex and were not pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy at last sex. Methods with established effectiveness — emergency contraception and the copper IUD — accounted for 8.9%, while 16.1% used a strategy with no medical basis, most commonly praying at 9.4%. Use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods, and contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with it.
items.why: Your Lecture 1 opens with a sexual-illiteracy poll. This is a 2025 nationally representative replacement, and “9.4% prayed” will land harder than any percentage currently on the slide.

items.finding: Problematic pornography use is the most common presentation of compulsive sexual behavior disorder, and many adults seeking help report that it began in adolescence — but adolescent prevalence had barely been measured. This cross-sectional study surveyed a representative sample of 3,106 Swedish third-year senior high school students, defining problematic use as self-reported difficulty refraining from or stopping. 10.4% reported it overall, with a large gender split: 18.8% of boys versus 3.9% of girls. It was associated with more time spent viewing, greater exposure to violent or otherwise concerning content, abusive experiences, mental health problems, risky behavior and non-suicidal self-injury.
items.why: Your slide says “1 in 3 teens believe porn has negatively influenced them,” which is a belief measure. This gives measured prevalence, a large gender split and a correlate profile from a representative sample.

items.finding: Thematic analysis of 31 in-depth interviews with heterosexual men aged 18–32 who came of age in what the authors call the age of consent. The most striking finding was how rarely these men described enjoying sex at all. Three overlapping themes emerged: anxiety and vigilance during encounters, moral concern about causing harm to a partner, and shame arising as much from self-criticism as from any accusation. The authors describe an inward turn in which a cultural suspicion of men has been internalized, so the operative question becomes not only "does she want this?" but "am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?" One participant described sex as like trying to defuse a bomb.
items.why: An uncomfortable, high-quality counterpoint about what consent education can feel like from the inside. Excellent discussion material for a mixed-gender classroom precisely because it complicates the standard framing.

items.finding: Tests whether facial asymmetry predicts women's sexuality, measured both long-term via the three Sociosexual Orientation Inventory subscales (Behavior, Attitude, Desire) and currently via frequency and intensity items based on the Female Sexual Function Index. Simple correlations looked supportive: asymmetry related negatively to partners in the last year (ρ = −.23, 95% CI [−0.45, 0.01]), SOI Attitude (ρ = −.25) and sexual desire (ρ = −.21). But once place of residence — rural versus urban — was entered as a confounder, every one of those effects fell away (.42 < p < .91). The authors conclude that external conditions matter when studying correlates of facial asymmetry.
items.why: The most directly corrective item this month. Your symmetry slides state that symmetry signals health and drives mate selection; this shows how fast such correlates evaporate under one confound. It doubles as a research-methods moment for both courses.
items.caution: The correlations did not survive a single confound control. The teachable point is the fragility, not an effect.

items.finding: A 2025 cross-sectional survey of 367 heterosexual Australian adults aged 19–87 (mean 39.1; 52.5% men, 44.8% women), examining who engages with AI-generated pornography. 26.0% reported having used it, with moderate familiarity overall. Regression analyses showed men and younger participants were significantly more likely to be familiar with and to have used it. Ideological factors — religiosity and political orientation — were not associated with use, and neither were relational ones: relationship status, relationship satisfaction and sexual satisfaction all came back null. The authors characterize early uptake as concentrated among digitally curious younger men but ideologically broad.
items.why: Useful precisely because it undercuts the intuitive story that AI porn signals a troubled relationship.

items.finding: Asexuality is increasingly described as a spectrum, but how its dimensions actually cluster had not been examined. Using the 2021 Ace Community Survey (analytic N = 11,063), this study took a person-centered approach based on four dimensions: attraction frequency, desire to act on attraction, sex drive, and disposition toward sex. Latent profile analysis produced four groups — Sex-Averse Low-Attraction, Context-Dependent Low-Attraction, Higher-Frequency, and Sex-Favorable High-Attraction — which were then compared on perceived asexuality-related impairment across family relationships, socioeconomic disadvantage, social exclusion and health. Overall impairment was low, but the Higher-Frequency profile reported comparatively more across domains.
items.why: Asexuality appears nowhere in your current lecture set, though Lecture 1 advertises LGBT+ identities. A coverage gap with a large new study attached.

items.finding: Group sex is usually studied through STI risk alone, which strips harm reduction out of the community norms that surround it. This study used thematic analysis of interviews with 20 participants in southwestern British Columbia to map the full range of practices. Strategies ran before, during and after events and addressed physical, emotional and social risk: vetting attendees in advance, establishing explicit consent norms such as consent circles and color-coded bracelets, promoting STI prevention through regular testing and barrier use, and maintaining privacy afterward. The authors describe a collaborative culture of care balancing community trust against individual accountability.
items.why: A concrete modern example of consent infrastructure, fitting your BDSM negotiation material.

items.finding: A scoping review following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR, synthesizing 27 studies on how digital masculinity ideals and media exposure relate to male genital self-image. Five themes emerged, spanning measure development, sociocultural and digital media influences, psychological correlates, sexual health outcomes, and penile dysmorphic concerns with their interventions. Lower genital self-image was associated with higher anxiety, depressive symptoms, social appearance anxiety, body dissatisfaction and poorer sexual functioning. Social media, pornography and masculinity norms appeared to reinforce unrealistic ideals, though evidence on pornography's direct effects remained inconsistent. The literature is dominated by cross-sectional studies from high-income countries.
items.why: Your “45% of men want a bigger penis — linked with viewing porn” slide has no citation on it. This is the current review of exactly that literature.

items.finding: 151 couples completed measures of body appreciation and sexual function, analyzed with an actor–partner interdependence moderation model, in a sample deliberately including gender and sexually diverse couples who face elevated risk of sexual difficulty through minority stress. A person's body appreciation was negatively related to their own sexual function difficulties — and to their partner's difficulties, but only when that partner was heterosexual. Gender identity did not significantly moderate the associations. The authors read this as evidence that a partner's sexual orientation shapes how body appreciation travels across a couple.
items.why: Dyadic evidence for the body-shame mechanism you already invoke to explain the orgasm gap — and it includes gender-diverse couples.

items.finding: Research on older adults' sexual health has grown, but the role of sexual distress in aging well sexually had not been systematically assessed. This 2024 online survey of 598 partnered, sexually active German adults aged 65 and over measured positive sexual aging with the Successful Sexual Aging Scale. Structural equation modeling controlling for age found that distress about sexual functioning was strongly and negatively associated with successful sexual aging in both women and men. Concerns about one's sex life carried an additional, unique association with lower scores among women only.
items.why: Your Lecture 11 effectively stops at the transition to parenthood. Sexual aging is a clean coverage gap.

items.finding: Examines what actually drives improvement in eSense, a digital tool delivering mindfulness-based therapy or CBT for female sexual interest/arousal disorder. 129 women were randomized to an arm (mean age 44.8 in MBT, 41.9 in CBT) and assessed at baseline, mid-treatment, post-treatment and six-month follow-up. Decreases in depressive and PTSD symptoms accompanied improvements in desire and distress in the mindfulness arm, while reductions in avoidance of sexual activity accompanied improvement in both arms. Higher treatment expectations predicted greater gains in the CBT arm only, whereas partner involvement, homework completion and number of modules finished predicted gains in both.
items.why: Mechanism detail for your vaginismus and sexual-dysfunction treatment slides — and avoidance reduction as the common pathway is the teachable point.

items.finding: Tests whether the link between social media use and openness to "sugar relationships" — treated here as one expression of a broader orientation toward sexual–economic exchange — holds uniformly across countries or depends on national norms. Using 22,292 adult women from 22 countries and Bayesian multilevel modeling, with measurement invariance assessed and alignment procedures applied beforehand, social media use was positively associated with openness, and modestly more so in culturally looser countries. Models including that interaction outperformed alternatives using country-level covariates such as digital infrastructure, socioeconomic structure and internet freedom, though the interaction effect itself was modest.
items.why: Fits your sexual–economic exchange and cultural-norms material with real cross-national scale.

items.finding: Research on sexual behavior in nightlife settings has concentrated on harassment and violence. This study asked instead why Spanish university students flirt in those venues, drawing on nine focus groups and 20 individual interviews. Flirtation turned out to serve several purposes well beyond playfulness or signaling interest: seeking immediate pleasure, hooking up, working through a current or former relationship, and acquiring sexual capital. The authors frame flirtation as a complicated skill that students value highly while also finding precarious and at times a source of harm.
items.why: Broadens your flirting section past signal-detection into what flirting is actually for.

items.finding: Non-erotic thoughts intrude during sex and have been linked to sexual dysfunction, but no work had asked whether they vary by culture. Two independent Prolific samples of White and second-generation South Asian women in Canada, the USA and the UK (N = 301; N = 284) completed a modified version of Purdon and Holdaway's measure. Overall frequency and anxiety did not differ between groups. Two categories did differ robustly across both samples — morality/guilt/regret and pregnancy/STI/health concerns — with South Asian women reporting both higher frequency and higher anxiety, effect sizes d = .24–.53. The authors conclude cultural influence here is domain-specific rather than global.
items.why: Cultural variation in a mechanism your arousal lecture treats as universal.

items.finding: Extends the safe-haven concept to people maintaining more than one committed relationship at once. 186 people practicing polyamory, separated from at least one partner while cohabiting with another, were surveyed between March and May 2020. Attachment anxiety and avoidance each negatively predicted satisfaction within both the cohabiting and the separated relationship. Attachment anxiety toward either partner predicted greater COVID distress, while avoidance worked in opposite directions depending on the partner — lowering distress toward a cohabiting partner, raising it toward a separated one. One cross-relationship effect emerged: attachment anxiety toward a separated partner predicted increased commitment to the cohabiting one.
items.why: Extends your attachment-pairings material beyond the dyad.

items.finding: A descriptive qualitative study of how breastfeeding reshapes sexuality, based on semi-structured interviews with 10 mothers (4 primiparous, 6 multiparous, mean age 29) between the third and sixth months postpartum. Three themes emerged — avoidance of sexuality, maintaining sexuality as a responsibility, and coping with breastfeeding's effects — across six subthemes covering physical and psychological changes in sexual dynamics, religious, social and cultural influences, fulfillment of the female role, changing perceptions of breasts, and coping strategies. Sexuality was often perceived as inappropriate during this period on cultural and religious grounds, and mothers' attempts to balance the two frequently produced emotional distress.
items.why: n=10. Small, but on a topic your lecture raises (lactation) and then drops.

items.finding: Cis- and heteronormative assumptions built into standard instruments undermine valid measurement of sexual function in sexual orientation and gender diverse populations. This scoping review searched PubMed, EBSCOhost and Web of Science and found 15 articles developing or validating inclusive instruments, with two reviewers independently screening and grading. Non-binary individuals were included in only one study. Most instruments reported adequate content and structural validity and internal consistency, but evidence for cross-gender, cross-orientation, cross-cultural, criterion and construct validity was lacking or unclear, and little was reported on test-retest reliability, measurement error or responsiveness to change. Most were validated in narrowly defined subgroups or covered a single domain.
items.why: A measurement complement to your history-of-sex-research lecture.

items.finding: Women who undergo risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy lose the ability to produce their own estradiol, raising two questions: whether their poorer sexual health traces to that loss, and whether estradiol therapy restores it. This study combined online questionnaires with qualitative interviews among BRCA1/2 variant carriers with and without estradiol therapy, comparing them to age-matched women with intact ovaries and women in spontaneous menopause. Those with the surgery had lower total sexual function scores and more sexually related distress. Interviews mirrored the numbers — pain, loss of desire, dryness — and added concerns about identity, relational strain, and not having been told what to expect. Estradiol therapy did not appear to resolve all of it.
items.why: Connects your fertility and hormone material to a real clinical population.

items.finding: A 2025 nationally representative survey of English-speaking American adults repeated a series of questions identical to those asked in 2018 about adolescents with gender dysphoria undergoing medical transition for gender affirmation. Support fell significantly over the seven years. The authors decompose this into cross-sectional differences, period change and change within birth cohorts, finding significant increases in disagreement among every age cohort born in 1988 or earlier. Given the shifted landscape, they then re-examine which characteristics predict support.
items.why: Contested terrain — your call on framing. As an attitude-change datapoint the design is straightforward; Regnerus’s broader work is widely contested.
items.caution: Contested literature. The design is straightforward as attitude-change data, but Regnerus's broader work is widely disputed. Your call on framing.

items.finding: A conceptual article addressed to mental health professionals, prompted by increasing reports of people who detransition or express regret after medical gender-affirming treatment. The authors note these experiences are heterogeneous, but that some individuals describe substantial adverse physical consequences and psychological distress stemming from the treatment they received. They argue a PTSD diagnosis as set out in DSM-5-TR may apply to some who have detransitioned, and discuss the relevance of moral injury, recently incorporated into DSM-5-TR under code Z65.8, for this population.
items.why: Contested terrain — your call on framing. Conceptual rather than empirical; flagged for awareness, not recommended.
items.caution: Contested literature. Conceptual rather than empirical. Flagged for awareness, not recommended.

items.finding: Catalogs the policies the U.S. administration established immediately after taking office in 2025 — restricting transgender rights and social legitimacy, curtailing youth access to gender-affirming care, terminating federal research and data collection on sexual and gender diversity, and restricting discussion of it in schools. The authors argue these pose a greater threat to sexual- and gender-minority health than earlier state-level policies because of their scope, speed and scale, and because they write animus into federal law. Drawing on structural stigma research, they forecast consequences through institutional change, increased minority stress, decreased social safety and behavioral change, identify subpopulations at disproportionate risk, and conclude that increasing social support and connection is the most feasible countermeasure.
items.why: Offered as balance in the same window for the two items above, so Lecture 4 can be taught from more than one position.
items.caution: Offered as balance in the same window for the two items above.

narrative.intro:
Every item below carries a real DOI pulled from Crossref, Europe PMC or OpenAlex. Nothing here is reconstructed from memory. Where an abstract was unavailable, that is stated rather than guessed at.

Each article appears in exactly one category, and once, under the course it serves most directly — any other course it touches is noted on the line.

cross_course.serves: PSY157 L10 (lie detection) and PSY170 L11 (persuasion)
PSY170 L13 (the E in EPOCH) and PSY157 L5 (communication)
PSY157 L3, PSY175 L8 and PSY170 L3

coverage: **No abstract available for 30 items**, concentrated in *Nature Reviews Psychology* (13 — mostly short research-highlight pieces with no abstract deposited anywhere), *Psychology of Sexual Orientation and Gender Diversity* (6, APA, poorly indexed), and the two Elsevier I-O titles. Titles and authors were captured; retrieve through the library if a title looks essential.

***Psychological Science in the Public Interest*** published nothing this window. Expected — it runs about three articles a year. It stays on the list because when it does publish, it is directly teachable.

**Abstract coverage is publisher-dependent.** Wiley and SAGE deposit to Crossref; Springer, Taylor & Francis and APA show up in Europe PMC; Elsevier appears in neither and is only partly covered by OpenAlex. Cascading all three reached 82% this month.
gaps: PSY175 lectures **7, 13, 14 and 15** are absent from the folder. Only 1–6, 8–12 and 16 are present, so matches cannot be proposed for roughly a quarter of that course.
**Asexuality / the ace spectrum** appears nowhere in the indexed lectures, though PSY175 Lecture 1 advertises LGBT+ identities and this month brought an N = 11,063 study.
**Sexual aging** past the transition to parenthood is absent from PSY175 Lecture 11.
narrative.retractions_none: Nothing qualified this month, which is the expected outcome in most months. The closest candidate was the facial asymmetry study, but it reports a null on a different claim (asymmetry → sexuality) than the one on the slide (symmetry → attractiveness), so it sits in Priority as a correction rather than a retraction. A single null result does not clear this bar; it takes a serious replication failure or a reversal of an accepted effect.
